concepts.name: Constitutional and Legal Status of Planning Commission vs NITI Aayog
key_dimensions: Neither body has constitutional backing — both created by executive resolution (Cabinet Resolution 1950 vs Cabinet Resolution 2015)
UPSC trap: Neither is a statutory body — no Act of Parliament governs either
Implications of non-constitutional status: no power to direct states, no enforcement mechanism
Contrast with Finance Commission which has constitutional backing under Article 280

concepts.name: Mandate and Core Functions: Allocation vs Advisory Role
key_dimensions: Planning Commission had quasi-judicial power to allocate funds to states via Five Year Plans
NITI Aayog is purely an advisory/think-tank body with NO fund allocation powers
UPSC trap: NITI Aayog cannot allocate or transfer resources to states — this power now lies with Finance Ministry and Finance Commission
Shift from 'Command and Control' planning to 'Cooperative and Competitive Federalism'

concepts.name: Five Year Plans vs Strategy/Vision Documents
key_dimensions: Planning Commission produced Five Year Plans (12 total, last was 12th Plan 2012–17)
NITI Aayog replaced FYPs with: Vision Document (15-year), Strategy Document (7-year), and Action Agenda (3-year)
UPSC trap: India's last Five Year Plan was the 12th Plan (2012–2017); NITI Aayog did NOT produce a 13th Plan
Shift from rigid central planning to flexible, iterative goal-setting aligned with SDGs

concepts.name: Composition and Chairmanship of Both Bodies
key_dimensions: Planning Commission: PM as Chairman, Deputy Chairman was effective head (Cabinet Minister rank), Full-time members
NITI Aayog: PM as Chairperson, CEO (Secretary-level officer) handles day-to-day, Vice-Chairperson is key policy figure
UPSC trap: Deputy Chairman of Planning Commission held Cabinet rank; NITI Aayog's Vice-Chairperson does NOT automatically hold Cabinet rank
New additions in NITI Aayog: Governing Council (all CMs + LG of UTs), Regional Councils (ad hoc)

concepts.name: Governing Council and Regional Councils of NITI Aayog
key_dimensions: Governing Council: All State Chief Ministers + Lt. Governors of UTs with legislature — a unique federal consultation forum
Regional Councils: Formed for specific cross-state issues (e.g., river water disputes, infrastructure corridors) — convened ad hoc
Planning Commission had NO equivalent of the Governing Council — NDC (National Development Council) was separate
UPSC trap: NDC was separate from Planning Commission; in NITI Aayog, the Governing Council subsumes the role of NDC

concepts.name: National Development Council (NDC) and Its Fate
key_dimensions: NDC was set up in 1952 separately from Planning Commission — comprised PM, all CMs, and Planning Commission members
NDC approved Five Year Plans and gave them political legitimacy
NITI Aayog's Governing Council effectively replaces NDC — but NDC was never formally abolished
UPSC trap: NDC still technically exists but is defunct; it has not been convened since NITI Aayog's formation

concepts.name: Center-State Financial Relations: Discretionary Grants and the Gadgil Formula
key_dimensions: Planning Commission distributed central assistance to states using the Gadgil Formula (later Gadgil-Mukherjee Formula)
Formula weighted by population, per capita income, fiscal performance, and special problems
NITI Aayog has no role in this distribution — devolution now governed by Finance Commission recommendations
UPSC trap: 14th Finance Commission increased states' share in divisible pool to 42% (from 32%), partly compensating for loss of plan transfers

concepts.name: Cooperative vs Competitive Federalism as NITI Aayog's Framework
key_dimensions: Cooperative Federalism: Joint forums (Governing Council), shared national goals, collaborative policy-making
Competitive Federalism: State rankings, indices (e.g., SDG India Index, Innovation Index, Export Preparedness Index) to incentivize performance
Planning Commission was accused of undermining federalism via conditional central transfers and one-size-fits-all planning
UPSC trap: NITI Aayog promotes both — 'cooperative AND competitive' federalism, not just one

concepts.name: NITI Aayog's Role in SDG Localization
key_dimensions: NITI Aayog is the nodal body for SDG implementation and monitoring in India
Publishes SDG India Index annually to rank states and UTs on SDG progress
Planning Commission had no SDG mandate (SDGs adopted in 2015, same year NITI Aayog was formed)
Links India's Vision 2047 (Viksit Bharat) with SDG 2030 goals — overlapping timelines require strategic alignment

concepts.name: Think-Tank Model vs Technocratic Planning Model
key_dimensions: Planning Commission operated as a technocratic central planner with top-down resource allocation authority
NITI Aayog modeled as a 'think tank' — generates policy research, pilots, best-practice dissemination
Key NITI Aayog outputs: policy papers, index reports, Atal Innovation Mission, pilot projects
UPSC trap: NITI Aayog lacks implementation authority — it can recommend but not direct ministries or states

concepts.name: Atal Innovation Mission (AIM) Under NITI Aayog
key_dimensions: AIM is India's flagship innovation promotion program housed under NITI Aayog
Key components: Atal Tinkering Labs (ATLs) in schools, Atal Incubation Centres (AICs), Atal New India Challenges
Represents NITI Aayog's operational role — a rare instance where it has a direct program mandate
UPSC trap: AIM is under NITI Aayog, NOT under DST or Ministry of Education — common confusion point

concepts.name: Criticism of Planning Commission: Reasons for Abolition
key_dimensions: Overcentralization: Imposed uniform plans ignoring regional diversity and state-specific needs
Parallel power center: Deputy Chairman wielded influence rivaling Finance Ministry, causing coordination issues
Inefficiency: Incremental budgeting, poor project appraisal, cost and time overruns normalized
Federalism concerns: States treated as subordinates; conditional grants distorted state priorities

concepts.name: Criticisms and Limitations of NITI Aayog
key_dimensions: Toothless advisory body: No power to enforce recommendations on states or Union ministries
States lose bargaining power: Under Planning Commission, states could negotiate plan allocations; no such forum now
Dominated by Union government perspective: Critics argue it still reflects Centre's priorities despite federal rhetoric
Accountability gap: No clear mechanism to assess whether NITI Aayog's advice is implemented or ignored

concepts.name: Role in Public Investment and Capital Formation
key_dimensions: Planning Commission was central to determining public investment priorities across sectors (agriculture, industry, infrastructure)
NITI Aayog's National Investment Pipeline (NIP) — ₹111 lakh crore infrastructure plan — is advisory in nature
PM GatiShakti National Master Plan (2021) operationalizes infrastructure coordination, but sits outside NITI Aayog
UPSC trap: PM GatiShakti is coordinated by DPIIT (Dept of Promotion of Industry), NOT NITI Aayog

concepts.name: Sectoral Policy Verticals of NITI Aayog
key_dimensions: NITI Aayog has thematic verticals: Agriculture, Education, Health, Industry, Natural Resources, Governance, etc.
It formulates transformation strategies — e.g., National Education Policy inputs, Agricultural reforms recommendations
Distinction: NITI Aayog recommends; line ministries implement — unlike Planning Commission which had approval authority
Notable outputs: Draft National Energy Policy, Zero Budget Natural Farming promotion, Electric Vehicles roadmap

concepts.name: Planning Commission's Project Appraisal vs NITI Aayog's Evaluation Role
key_dimensions: Planning Commission's Programme Evaluation Organisation (PEO) evaluated government schemes
Under NITI Aayog, Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office (DMEO) was created by merging PEO and Independent Evaluation Office (IEO)
IEO was set up in 2013 (during UPA-II) as an independent evaluator — merged into DMEO under NITI Aayog
UPSC trap: DMEO is under NITI Aayog but maintains notional independence; it evaluates Centrally Sponsored Schemes

concepts.name: Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS): Rationalization and NITI Aayog's Role
key_dimensions: Planning Commission proliferated CSS without adequate state consultation — states complained of tied, conditional funds
NITI Aayog recommended rationalization of CSS — Sub-Group of CMs report (2015) suggested reducing CSS and giving states more flexibility
Post-2015: CSS restructured into Core (fully funded by Centre) and Core of Core (higher centre share) categories
UPSC trap: NITI Aayog recommended rationalization but the actual restructuring was done by the Finance Ministry/Cabinet

concepts.name: Viksit Bharat @2047 and NITI Aayog's Long-Term Vision Role
key_dimensions: Viksit Bharat @2047 is India's vision to become a developed nation by its centenary of Independence
NITI Aayog is anchoring the long-term strategy document for Viksit Bharat — links to its 15-year vision mandate
Four pillars: Yuva (Youth), Garib (Poor), Mahila (Women), Annadata (Farmer)
UPSC trap: Viksit Bharat is a government-wide initiative — NITI Aayog provides the framework but implementation spans all ministries

concepts.name: Comparison with Global Planning/Advisory Bodies
key_dimensions: Planning Commission compared to Soviet-style Gosplan — centralized, target-based, supply-driven planning
NITI Aayog compared to global think tanks: South Korea's KDI, UK's Cabinet Office Strategy Unit
UPSC angle: India's shift mirrors global trend away from central planning toward evidence-based policy advisory
Key difference from Finance Commission: Finance Commission is constitutional, quasi-judicial, periodic — NITI Aayog is permanent, advisory, executive

concepts.name: Distinction Between NITI Aayog, Finance Commission, and Finance Ministry in Resource Devolution
key_dimensions: Finance Commission (Art. 280): Constitutionally mandated, determines vertical and horizontal devolution of taxes to states
Finance Ministry: Controls Union Budget, borrowing limits of states (FRBM), and Centrally Sponsored Scheme funding
NITI Aayog: No role in resource transfer — only policy advisory and strategic planning
UPSC trap: Post-abolition of Planning Commission, states lost a negotiating platform for plan funds — Finance Commission now more critical, but it too is periodic (every 5 years)
